content: Epilepsy is a neurological condition that affects both children and adults. It is characterized by epileptic seizures, which occur due to excessive and abnormal electrical activity in the cortical cells of the brain. Concerns have been raised that current epilepsy care for children has limited impact on long-term outcomes. In response, healthcare professionals and administrators have developed various service models and strategies to address these perceived shortcomings. This document is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2018. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of specialized or dedicated interventions for epilepsy compared to usual care in children and adolescents with epilepsy, as well as their families. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted on January 14, 2020, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The CRS Web also includes the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialised Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Experts in the field were contacted for information on unpublished and ongoing studies, and the websites of epilepsy organizations and reference lists of included studies were reviewed. The review included randomized controlled trials that recruited children and adolescents with epilepsy. Two independent reviewers selected the trials for inclusion and extracted relevant data. The outcomes assessed included seizure frequency and severity, appropriateness and volume of prescribed medications (including evidence of drug toxicity), participants' knowledge of information and advice received from professionals, participants' reports of health and quality of life, objective measures of general health status, objective measures of social or psychological functioning (such as days missed from school or work and employment status), and costs of care or treatment. The results of data extraction and quality assessment were presented in structured tables and as a narrative summary. Summary statistics for each outcome were also extracted. The review included nine studies evaluating eight interventions, which consisted of seven distinct self-management programs aimed at educating or counseling children with epilepsy and their parents, as well as one new model of care. Most of the outcomes were based on self-reported data. Each program demonstrated some benefits for the well-being of children with epilepsy, but all included studies had methodological flaws. None of the programs were evaluated across different study samples, and no outcome was measured and reported consistently across studies. This lack of consistency precluded the possibility of conducting a meta-analysis, even if the interventions were deemed similar enough to combine in such an analysis. The outcomes deemed important for decision-making about the interventions were selected based on guidance from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that one educational intervention reduced seizure frequency. Low-certainty evidence indicated that two other educational interventions reduced seizure severity, improved seizure control, and increased seizure cure rates. However, the evidence for other outcomes, such as medication adherence, knowledge, self-efficacy, and the perceived impact of epilepsy on quality of life, was mixed. In conclusion, while each of the evaluated programs showed some benefits for children with epilepsy, their impact was highly variable. No single program demonstrated benefits across the full range of outcomes, and all studies had methodological limitations. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to recommend any one program over others. Further research, particularly randomized controlled trials using validated measures and considering both clinical meaningfulness and statistical significance, is needed to provide more robust evidence.
